sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Orientation, facilitation questions, tone guidance, and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Unit 10 opens Grounding — Pillar 3 of the DIG framework. The central question is systemic: is the organisation's operating system configured to sustain what Direction defined and Influence mobilised? Most strategies fail because the internal operating conditions were never aligned to carry the weight of sustained execution.

This unit introduces the ESRG framework — Environment, Systems, Resources, Governance — as the four domains that collectively determine whether performance can be sustained over time. It also introduces two practical instruments: the Cultural Operating Code (translating values into measurable behavioural norms) and the ESRG Execution Scanner (the quarterly diagnostic that operationalises collective intelligence).

The Application exercise — Build the Cultural Operating Code — is the centrepiece. Protect the full 55 minutes. Teams must work with real values and leave with at least three draft norms they can actually use.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
“Most strategies that survive the first quarter fail by the third. What does that tell us about where execution actually breaks down?”
“Think of a value your organisation states. What would a leader who genuinely lives that value do differently from one who only states it? That difference is your Cultural Operating Code.”
“Which of the four ESRG domains is most misaligned with your current strategic direction — and how long has that misalignment been visible?”
“When your team completed the ESRG scanner individually and compared results — what pattern did you see that no single person could see alone?”
“A COC norm only becomes real when a leader uses it in a difficult conversation. Which norm from today will you use first — and when?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points

Watch for: the compliance response. When leaders see the ESRG framework, some immediately jump to “we already do this.” Push past self-assessment to evidence: “What would your team say if we asked them whether psychological safety actually exists in your function?”
Watch for: values that sound good but mean nothing. In the COC exercise, every norm must pass the pressure test — does it hold when a senior leader violates it, or does it only apply to junior staff?

Watch for: the ESRG scanner being treated as a performance report. Emphasise: this is a diagnostic. The purpose is intelligence. A leader who surfaces a HIGH breach is exercising exactly the discipline the unit teaches.

Timing: Awareness and Intelligence can move at pace. Extrapolating benefits from brief cross-functional discussion of which friction patterns are most recognisable. Reserve the full 55 minutes for Application.

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Introducing the four domains that determine whether performance can be sustained — and the conditions required for each to support consistent strategic delivery.
slo: Recognise the environment, systems, resources and governance conditions that sustain performance.
Explain how shared behavioural norms shape the operating environment.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Awareness

Open with the hard question: “Is the organisation itself built to sustain this performance over time?” That framing immediately distinguishes Grounding from the previous pillars and establishes why this unit matters even when strategy is clear and leadership is committed.

The ESRG domain cards are the core of this section. Work through each card in turn. The E card is the richest — take extra time on the Behavioural Dimension, particularly the Cultural Operating Code. This concept connects directly to the Application exercise so it must land here first.

Close Awareness with the synthesis statement: a weakness in any one domain creates friction the other three cannot fully compensate for. That is the interdependence principle that underpins everything that follows.

parts.title: 1.1 — ESRG Alignment: The Grounding Question
content: Enterprise alignment is one of the most decisive success factors in strategy execution. Even the most carefully designed strategy will struggle to deliver consistent results if the organisation's internal operating conditions are not configured to support it.

This programme builds on the Freedman & Elliott model for high-performance cultures, which recognises that performance is sustained by the organisational system that surrounds the strategy — the environment people work in, the systems they rely on, the resources they are given, and the governance structures that guide decisions and enforce accountability.

When ESRG alignment is present, execution becomes coordinated, predictable, and scalable. When alignment is absent, friction appears — delays, confusion, rework, decision bottlenecks, and capability gaps that gradually erode execution momentum until strategic intent and operational reality are no longer recognisable as the same thing.

parts.title: 1.2 — The Four ESRG Domains
content: E
Environment
Physical & Behavioural Conditions
Environment determines whether people can perform their work efficiently, safely, and collaboratively — across two inseparable dimensions.
Dimension 1
Physical
Dimension 2
Behavioural
Infrastructure
Reliable connectivity, equipment, and working spaces for everyone
Facilities maintenance responsive enough to prevent structural workarounds
Business continuity provisions so infrastructure failure does not halt execution
Workspace Design
Physical layout that reduces delays between dependent roles — proximity is a performance variable
Collaboration zones and quiet zones that reflect the work the strategy demands
Visual signals reflecting current strategic priorities
Operational Conditions
Remote and hybrid staff participating equally — two-tier participation creates two-tier accountability
Workspaces supporting all people without requiring advocacy for basic functionality
Ergonomic and recovery spaces — physical wellbeing is a capacity issue
Values
Values must be demonstrable — translated into observable, specific behaviours
Values must be embedded in 360-degree feedback — assessing how as well as what
Values must be enforced through consequences consistently regardless of seniority
Cultural Operating Code
For each value, a named acronym-based norm defining observable, repeatable behaviour
Norms must be explicit, modelled, reinforced, and reviewed periodically
The COC is the behavioural architecture of the organisation
Psychological Conditions
Psychological safety so people surface problems early
Protection from aggression, disrespect, or hostility — safety is a performance condition
Onboarding that transmits culture deliberately — culture is either taught or it defaults
S
Systems
Operational Infrastructure of Execution
Systems determine how work flows, how progress is tracked, and how coordination happens across teams and functions.
Process Clarity
Core processes documented, current, and easy to find
Handoffs between teams mapped and visible with clearly defined roles
Data Integrity
A trusted single source of truth for key operational data
Reporting that reflects operational reality
Workflow Visibility
Teams can see where work sits in the end-to-end process
Dashboards update fast enough to support real-time decision-making
System Integration
Systems communicate to eliminate duplicate work and data inconsistency
Shadow systems and informal trackers controlled and rationalised
Governance Integration
Approvals and sign-offs simple, time-bound, and traceable within the system
Compliance checks embedded in the workflow
R
Resources
Capability Capacity of the Organisation
Resources determine whether the organisation has the human, financial, and operational capacity to deliver strategic commitments without degrading its people or performance quality.
Workforce Capacity
Staffing levels supporting normal and peak demand without chronic overload
Burnout is a strategic risk
Capability Alignment
Skills matching current work requirements with talent planning anticipating future needs
Training accompanying every change in process, system, or strategic direction
Financial Support
Budget available for critical strategic initiatives
Bureaucratic delays to operational investment are a governance failure
Operational Resilience
Backup coverage for critical roles
Knowledge transfer before key staff rotate or exit — institutional knowledge must not reside in individuals
Employee Sustainability
Teams able to signal unsustainable workloads early — before performance degrades or talent exits
Administrative support so specialists focus on high-value work
G
Governance
Accountability & Decision Discipline
Governance ensures that execution remains visible, accountable, and actively managed — and that the organisation's decision-making architecture supports strategic momentum.
Clear Accountability
Each area of strategic work has a clearly assigned owner
Delegation matches responsibility with commensurate authority — accountability without authority is a structural failure
Decision Authority
Decision rights clearly defined, communicated, and understood at every level
Approval chains short enough to support the pace the strategy demands
Execution Oversight
Review forums that make decisions and drive accountability
Risk discussions accompanying performance discussions as a standard discipline
Ethical Integrity
Leaders modelling the ethical behaviour and fairness they expect of others
Consequences applied consistently regardless of seniority — selective enforcement destroys credibility
Governance Adaptability
Governance structures evolving as operating conditions and strategy change
Governance fit for a previous era must be updated

parts.title: 1.3 — ESRG Synthesis
content: Environment → enables the behavioural and physical conditions for productive, safe, values-aligned work
Systems → enable efficient, visible, and coordinated execution flow
Resources → provide the human, financial, and operational capacity to deliver
Governance → ensures accountability, decision discipline, and execution oversight

The organisation's sustained execution capacity depends on the synchronisation of these four domains. A weakness in any one domain creates friction that the other three cannot fully compensate for. The discipline of ESRG Alignment is the discipline of ensuring all four are working together — coherently, continuously, and in direct service of the strategic direction.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why ESRG Alignment Drives Sustained Execution
sections.sub: Understanding how each ESRG domain removes a specific category of friction — and seeing the discipline in action through two worked examples: the Cultural Operating Code and the ESRG Execution Scanner.
slo: Explain how each organisational domain removes a specific source of friction from execution.
Assess where operating conditions support or constrain strategic priorities.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Intelligence

This section has two worked examples — use them both as live teaching moments. Walk through the COC example to demonstrate what the translation discipline produces before participants attempt it in Application. Walk through the Scanner example to show what collective intelligence looks like before they use the tool.

For the Scanner: the key insight is Steps 3 and 4 — the COMPASS frequency map and the three overlapping themes. Emphasise that no individual leader could see these patterns alone. The power of the scan is collective.

The ignition point statement at the end of the enabling conditions section is important: when all four ESRG domains work together, execution no longer depends on leadership attention or individual heroism. That is the promise of Grounding.

parts.title: 2.1 — The ESRG Ignition Point: How Each Domain Enables Execution
content: Sustained execution begins when the organisation's operating conditions actively support the work required to deliver the strategy. Strategic intent provides direction. Execution discipline provides movement. But sustained results emerge only when the enterprise system itself reinforces the work being done — consistently, structurally, and without dependence on heroic individual effort.
E
Enable the Work
S
Streamline the Flow
R
Resource the Strategy
G
Govern the Rhythm
The physical and behavioural conditions of work must both be active
The physical dimension enables the mechanics of execution — teams reaching each other quickly, hybrid participation equal, workspace design matching the work the strategy demands.

The behavioural dimension is equally critical. Values enable performance when they are demonstrable, measured, and enforced. They create a behavioural environment where conduct is as consequential as results. The Cultural Operating Code translates each value into a named, actionable norm — moving values from aspiration to operation. Psychological safety completes the enabling condition: when people can surface problems early, the organisation gains real-time intelligence about where execution is straining.
Systems must make execution visible — visibility is the precondition for accountability

Execution depends on how work travels from one function to another. When pathways are clear and reliable, teams can see where work sits, how it progresses, and what action is required next. Streamlined systems reduce duplication and ensure everyone operates from a shared source of truth.
Governance integration within systems — approvals, compliance checks, and escalation triggers embedded in the workflow — removes the friction that accumulates at every function boundary.
Resourcing the strategy means resourcing the people who carry it
Teams must possess the skills required, the capacity to sustain effort, and the tools to operate efficiently. Financial investment must flow to the initiatives that drive the strategy forward.

Employee sustainability is a resource alignment condition. Burnout degrades execution quality, accelerates talent exit, and erodes institutional knowledge that is often the organisation's most critical and least recoverable asset. Resourcing the strategy means resourcing people to perform over time.
Governance maintains the cadence of accountability that keeps work advancing

Execution requires a consistent rhythm of decisions, reviews, and accountability conversations. When governance is aligned, decision-making becomes predictable and responsive. Leaders convene forums that resolve problems.

Governance also carries the responsibility of ethical integrity. The governance system must apply its standards consistently — regardless of seniority, regardless of results. Leaders exempt from accountability by virtue of position or performance numbers destroy governance credibility faster than any single operational failure.

“When all four conditions operate together, execution no longer depends solely on leadership attention. The organisation's operating system begins to reinforce the work itself. That is the ignition point. That is Grounding.”

parts.title: 2.2 — Worked Example 1: The IBSL Cultural Operating Code
content: IBSL's values are: Intentionality · Integrity · Collaboration · Accountability · Excellence · Human-Centricity

The translation discipline: for each value, define the observable, repeatable behaviour that becomes the organisational way of life — expressed as a named acronym that is teachable, measurable, and replicable.
Intentionality
Leading with purpose, clarity, and discipline
AIM
Act with purpose · Interrogate assumptions · Maintain the discipline

Every leader is clear on the why behind every decision, challenges their own thinking before committing, and follows through with consistency. Intentionality is the discipline of knowing exactly why you are doing what you are doing, and holding that line when conditions make it inconvenient.

360 indicator: Before committing to any initiative, can this leader articulate the strategic purpose it serves, the assumption they are making, and the specific standard they will hold themselves to in executing it?
Integrity
Consistency between words, behaviour, and outcomes
SAY
Say what you mean · Act on what you say · Yield the truth regardless of consequence

Integrity is about consistency between word, behaviour, and outcome — even when telling the truth is uncomfortable, even when the outcome is not what was promised. What we say and what we do are the same thing. Always.
360 indicator: Does this leader name what was promised, what was delivered, and what the gap cost — before being asked?
Collaboration
Leveraging diversity of thought and collective intelligence
ONE
Own a shared outcome · Navigate difference with respect · Execute as a unified force
Collaboration is the decision to produce something together that no single function could produce alone. The result belongs to the team.
360 indicator: Does this leader present the shared outcome — including what their function gave up to make it possible — or only their function's contribution?
Accountability
Owning results and reinforcing transparency
OAR
Own it · Act on it · Report it

Every commitment is owned by a named person, acted on within an agreed timeframe, and reported on honestly regardless of outcome. Accountability begins the moment a commitment is made. We report the truth and fix the gap.
360 indicator: Does this leader surface gaps the moment they become visible — with the cause, the impact, and the recovery action already identified?
Excellence
Upholding rigour, learning, and measurable impact
SET
Set the standard · Earn the evidence · Transform through learning

Excellence is a daily discipline. We define what good looks like, we measure whether we are achieving it, and we use every gap as a learning signal. It is about being better than last quarter, and proving it with evidence.
360 indicator: Can this leader answer three questions at any review: What standard did we set? What evidence do we have? What have we changed as a result?
Human-Centricity
Placing people at the core of leadership and execution
SEE
See the person behind the role · Enable growth deliberately · Ensure dignity in every interaction

Human-centricity is the commitment that leadership serves people. Every interaction must be conducted with the awareness that there is a person on the other side of it. We invest in growth. We protect dignity. We never reduce a person to their output.
360 indicator: Does this leader open with the person — their experience of the quarter, what supported them, what constrained them — before moving to the result?
IBSL COC SUMMARY
Value | Acronym | Norm
Intentionality | AIM | Act with purpose. Interrogate assumptions. Maintain the discipline.
Integrity | SAY | Say what you mean. Act on what you say. Yield the truth regardless of consequence.
Collaboration | ONE | Own a shared outcome. Navigate difference with respect. Execute as a unified force.
Accountability | OAR | Own it. Act on it. Report it.
Excellence | SET | Set the standard. Earn the evidence. Transform through learning.
Human-Centricity | SEE | See the person behind the role. Enable growth deliberately. Ensure dignity in every interaction.
AIM · SAY · ONE · OAR · SET · SEE

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the ESRG Friction Zones?
sections.sub: Recognising the predictable friction patterns in each ESRG domain — and understanding what type of organisational intervention is required to restore alignment.
slo: Recognise the institutional constraints and dependencies that create friction in each domain.
Determine the type of intervention each constraint requires.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Extrapolating

Open with the reframe: friction begins quietly, in small operational inconveniences that gradually accumulate. The discipline of Extrapolating is recognising these signals early — before they compound.

As you work through each friction domain, invite leaders to identify which friction pattern they recognise most immediately in their organisation. This primes them for the scanner exercise without requiring them to commit to a judgement.

The closing section — Seeing Friction as Organisational Intelligence — is the critical reframe. Emphasise: every instance of friction reveals something precise about the organisation's readiness. The executive team's role is to transform insights into targeted alignment actions.

parts.title: 3.1 — E · Environment Friction
content: Environment friction occurs across both dimensions. Both must be examined — addressing one without the other produces only partial restoration of execution conditions.
Physical Environment Friction

Teams are asked to work in new ways — cross-functional collaboration, faster decision cycles, hybrid engagement — yet the workspace continues to reflect older patterns. Offices organised around hierarchy. Meeting rooms not equipped for hybrid participation. Teams that depend on each other separated by organisational structures that make quick problem-solving unnecessarily difficult.
When physical environment friction exists, people spend energy navigating obstacles. The execution cost is real — and largely invisible in any performance report.
Behavioural Environment Friction

Values misalignment is one of the most common and least diagnosed sources of sustained execution failure. When stated values are not translated into observable, specific behaviours and not embedded in performance measurement, they function as decoration. The absence of a Cultural Operating Code means cultural expectations remain implicit — and implicit expectations are interpreted differently by different people at different seniority levels. That inconsistency is friction.

360-degree feedback gaps are a reliable indicator of values friction. When performance management assesses only what people delivered — and not how — the measurement system reinforces a culture in which conduct is invisible. High performers who undermine colleagues or avoid accountability are protected by their results. Over time this erodes the trust sustained execution depends on.

Psychological safety failures are a direct execution risk. When people hesitate to raise concerns, execution issues surface too late. When the cultural environment tolerates aggression, disrespect, or the silencing of dissent, the organisation loses its most valuable early warning system: the willingness of people to tell the truth about what is actually happening.

parts.title: 3.2 — S · Systems Friction
content: Many organisations attempt to run new strategic priorities through legacy operational systems. Workflows designed for previous business models remain unchanged even though the strategic direction now requires different forms of coordination, reporting, and decision speed. Teams must invent workarounds simply to keep work moving — and workarounds, over time, become the de facto system.

One of the most common forms of systems friction appears in data and reporting architecture. Teams rely on different data sources, dashboards measuring different definitions of performance, or reporting systems that update too slowly to inform real-time decisions. When this occurs, leaders spend more time debating the accuracy of information than interpreting what it means for execution. Data integrity is an execution problem.

Governance integration within systems is a frequently missed alignment condition. When approvals, compliance checks, and escalation triggers sit outside the workflow as separate, after-the-fact processes, they add latency at every function boundary. When systems friction is present, execution becomes dependent on informal coordination and individual effort.

parts.title: 3.3 — R · Resources Friction
content: Strategic plans frequently assume that the necessary capabilities already exist within the organisation. In reality, many strategies require skills that must be developed, technologies that must be acquired, or staffing levels that must expand. The assumption of readiness is itself a source of friction.

Capacity constraints represent a particularly damaging form of friction. Chronic understaffing forces teams to operate under constant pressure — increasing error rates, reducing attention to detail, and accelerating burnout. At its core, this is a strategic risk. Burnout degrades execution quality, accelerates talent exit, and erodes the institutional knowledge that is often the organisation's most critical and least recoverable asset.

Employee sustainability is therefore a resource alignment condition. The absence of a signal that workloads are unsustainable is evidence that psychological safety in the Resources domain is insufficient.

Financial misalignment is a structural contradiction many organisations sustain for longer than they realise. Strategy follows resources. Where the money goes is where the organisation's real priorities reside — regardless of what the strategy document states.

parts.title: 3.4 — G · Governance Friction
content: In many organisations, governance structures were originally designed to control risk, with little regard for execution speed. Governance that was fit for a previous strategic era — and has not been updated — is itself a source of friction.

Unclear decision rights produce one of the most visible and costly forms of governance friction. Teams are uncertain about who has the authority to approve a step forward, resulting in delays while decisions are escalated through multiple management layers. Decision rights that are not clearly defined at every level are a structural drag on execution velocity.

Ethical integrity failures are among the most corrosive and least visible sources of governance friction. When the governance system applies standards selectively — when high performers are exempt from accountability by virtue of results, when leaders modelling values misalignment are protected by seniority — the credibility of the governance system erodes. Selective enforcement weakens governance and delegitimises it. And a governance system that lacks legitimacy cannot sustain the execution discipline the strategy requires.

Leadership absence from execution oversight is often misread as a trust signal. Leaders who delegate governance entirely — absent from review forums, not engaging actively with accountability conversations — undermine the very structures they have commissioned.

parts.title: 3.5 — Seeing Friction as Organisational Intelligence
content: Recognising these friction patterns is about gaining operational intelligence.
Values misalignment in the environment signals a gap between cultural aspiration and cultural reality
Systems fragmentation signals an infrastructure built for a different strategic era
Capacity constraints signal a resource allocation that has not yet caught up with strategic ambition
Governance inconsistency signals a leadership system not yet operating at the standard the strategy demands

The role of the executive team is to transform those insights into targeted alignment actions that restore the conditions required for sustained performance — so that execution becomes a function of organisational design.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.h2: Cross-ESRG Architecture — Collective Intelligence of Execution
sections.sub: The Execution Muscle Scan — a structured quarterly leadership conversation that transforms individual observations into collective intelligence about execution readiness.
slo: Demonstrate an enterprise view of the operating conditions required for sustainable performance.
Formulate an enterprise agenda for aligning operating conditions with strategic priorities.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Integration

The Execution Muscle Scan is the practical instrument that makes this unit operational. Walk through all four reflections with the group using the mountain expedition metaphor as the framing device — the purpose is to ensure the expedition is still strong enough to keep climbing.
The COMPASS-ESRG table is the most important reference in this section. Spend time on it — this is the connection that ties Unit 9 and Unit 10 together as a coherent diagnostic system.

Close by naming the key insight: the output is a leadership instrument for proactive execution architecture. The Collated Executive View is what the team brings to the next performance review as evidence that they are engineering the conditions for sustained delivery.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Execution Muscle Scan
content: In a mountain expedition, climbers periodically stop to assess whether the conditions around them still support a safe and successful ascent. They check the terrain, the equipment, the team's condition, and the route ahead. The purpose is to ensure the expedition remains properly equipped to continue the climb.

The Execution Muscle Scan is a structured leadership conversation conducted during the quarterly progress review, immediately after performance has been examined. The executive team shifts its attention from outcomes to the conditions that enable those outcomes.
“Are the organisational conditions still supporting our ability to continue the climb?”

Through this process, the executive team transforms operational observations from across the organisation into collective intelligence about execution readiness — and identifies where the enterprise system must be strengthened before the next execution cycle begins.

parts.title: 4.2 — The Four Reflections
content: E
Environment
S
Systems
R
Resources
G
Governance
Enabling the Work — Physical & Behavioural

Physical: Can teams reach one another quickly? Are hybrid participants fully engaged — or experiencing two-tier participation that creates two-tier accountability? Do workspaces reflect current strategic priorities — or legacy signals from a previous planning cycle?

Behavioural: Are values being demonstrated in how leaders conduct themselves in reviews and performance conversations? Is the Cultural Operating Code being actively reinforced, or has it become background noise? Do people feel safe enough to surface execution problems early — or are they managing impressions and absorbing friction silently?
“Do the physical and behavioural conditions of our environment make it easy for people to collaborate, speak honestly, and advance the work?”
Streamlining the Flow

Are processes remaining clear, current, and accessible — or have workarounds accumulated to the point where the workaround has become the de facto system? Are data sources remaining trusted and consistently defined across functions — or are teams spending review time debating accuracy? Is workflow visibility sufficient — or is execution progress only visible through informal channels?
Are approvals, compliance checks, and escalation triggers embedded in the workflow — or do they sit outside it as separate, time-consuming layers that slow execution at every function boundary?
“Do our systems allow work, data, and decisions to move smoothly and visibly across the organisation?”
Resourcing the Strategy — Capability, Capacity & Sustainability

Do teams possess the skills required for the current phase? Are staffing levels sufficient for normal and peak demand? Is financial investment continuing to flow to the initiatives driving the strategy forward — or defaulting to historical allocation patterns?

Critically: are teams operating at a pace and load that can be maintained — or are they absorbing pressure that is quietly degrading performance quality, accelerating talent exit, and eroding institutional knowledge? Can people signal unsustainable workloads early — or has the culture made that signal feel too costly to send?
“Do our teams have the capability, capacity, and sustainability required to deliver the strategy over time?”
Maintaining the Rhythm — Decision, Accountability & Integrity

Are decision rights remaining clear at every level — or is approval ambiguity reintroducing decision bottlenecks? Are review forums functioning as decision forums — or have they reverted to status update sessions that produce reports with no actions?

Are accountability standards being applied consistently regardless of seniority or results? Is leadership presence in execution oversight active and visible — or has governance been delegated while leaders signal by absence that the process is optional? Are risk discussions happening alongside performance discussions — or only triggered by crisis?
“Are decisions, accountability, and ethical standards operating at the pace and consistency required to sustain execution?”

parts.title: 4.3 — The COMPASS-ESRG Connection
content: The Execution Muscle Scan connects directly to the COMPASS framework introduced in Unit 9. COMPASS locates where in the execution architecture friction is forming. ESRG diagnoses what type of organisational condition is causing it.
COMPASS Zone | Primary ESRG Domain | Friction Source
Clarity of Direction | Governance | Decision rights unclear; leadership avoiding difficult trade-offs
Organisational Alignment | Environment | Values misalignment; cultural norms fragmented across functions
Management Discipline | Governance | Review forums producing reports not decisions; accountability inconsistently enforced
People & Capability | Resources | Capability gaps; capacity constraints; employee sustainability failing
Allocation of Resources | Resources | Budget following history; funding pathways too slow
Systems & Execution | Systems | Legacy processes; data fragmentation; shadow systems accumulating
Sensing & Adaptation | Environment + Systems | Psychological safety absent; feedback loops broken; data not trusted
Together they enable the precision that moves leadership from reactive troubleshooting to proactive execution architecture — the foundation of the ESRG Scanner tool.

parts.title: 4.4 — Collective Signal Intelligence & The Outcome
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Closing Note — Integration

Close by naming the shift: the group has moved from reacting to execution friction to actively engineering the conditions for sustained delivery. The Enterprise ESRG Alignment Agenda is a leadership instrument. When these conditions remain aligned, the organisation is prepared to continue the climb. The destination remains the same. The expedition becomes stronger with every deliberate step forward.
content: The power of the Execution Muscle Scan lies in how it combines signals from across the executive team into a shared picture of execution readiness. An operational challenge visible to one executive may reflect a systems issue identified by another. A capability concern raised by one function may connect to a governance constraint recognised by another. A values misalignment observed in one team may be a downstream consequence of a leadership behaviour pattern that is visible across multiple functions — but only named when leaders look at the picture collectively.

When those signals are shared in the structured format of the scan, they reveal patterns that individual leaders cannot see alone. Individual observation becomes collective intelligence — a shared understanding of where the organisation's execution conditions must be strengthened before friction compounds into failure.

The output is a Collated Executive View — a shared picture of where the organisation's ESRG conditions are strong, where they are straining, and where targeted intervention is required before the next execution cycle begins.

parts.title: 4.5 — Enterprise ESRG Alignment Agenda: Collective Capture
content: Each leader contributes one ESRG friction observation to a shared, structured agenda — replacing informal complaint with collective intelligence the leadership team can act on by function.

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.sub: Teams translate organisational values into observable, teachable, measurable norms — producing a Cultural Operating Code that leadership can use to reinforce, recognise, and correct behaviour consistently across the organisation.
slo: Translate organisational values into observable behavioural norms that support accountable performance.
Commit to applying one norm in the next difficult leadership conversation.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Application

This exercise is the centrepiece of Unit 10. Protect all 55 minutes. Teams must work with values real enough that the translation work is honest. The three value sets are designed to cover distinct organisational characters — ensure different teams work different sets where numbers allow.
Watch for acronyms that are clever but not useful. Redirect: “Start with the behaviour. The acronym is only the packaging.”

Watch for norms that only describe comfortable situations. The test is whether the norm holds when a senior leader violates it, when a high performer contradicts it, when telling the truth is costly. If it doesn't hold under pressure, it is a preference.
Watch for norms that are too generic. If Transparency and Integrity produce the same norm, the translation work is not done. Push until the norm is specific to the value.

Use the facilitator reference COC at the bottom of this section during the debrief. The full worked examples across all three value sets are there for comparison and coaching, and stay with the facilitator.

parts.title: 5.2 — The Exercise (55 minutes)
guidance: ◆ Key Considerations for Each Norm
Is the norm specific enough to use in a performance conversation?
Could it appear in a 360-degree feedback instrument?
Would every function in the organisation interpret it the same way?
content: Part 1 · 5 min
Choose Your Set
Part 2 · 35 min
Build the COC
Part 3 · 15 min
COC Challenge
Choose Your Value Set
Each team selects one value set. No two teams should work with the same set where numbers allow — the debrief is richer when different sets are presented in the room.
Build the Cultural Operating Code from the values in your chosen set. You will not complete all six in session — choose the three that feel most relevant or most challenging to translate.
Build the COC — 35 Minutes
Work through three values from your chosen set. For each value:
Step 1 — Define the behaviour
Ask: “What would a leader who genuinely lives this value do differently from one who only states it?” Write the answer as a specific, observable behaviour.
Step 2 — Build the acronym

Take the first letter of three action words that capture the behaviour. Each word must be an observable action — a verb the leader performs. The acronym must be memorable enough to use in a corridor conversation.
Step 3 — Write the norm statement

One sentence explaining what the value means in daily practice — specific enough that a new employee reading it on Day 1 would know exactly what behaviour will be recognised and what will be corrected.
The COC Challenge — 15 Minutes Full Group
Each team presents their strongest single norm from the three they worked on — the one they found most powerful or most difficult to translate.
The full group applies three tests:
Test 1 — The New Employee Test
“If a new employee read this norm on their first day, would they know exactly what behaviour will be recognised and what will be corrected?”
Test 2 — The Pressure Test
“Does this norm hold when a senior leader violates it? Or does it only apply to junior staff?”
Test 3 — The Mirror Test
“Would every person in this room be comfortable being assessed against this norm in their own 360-degree feedback?”

“A Cultural Operating Code only becomes real the moment a leader uses it in a difficult conversation — when they name the norm that was breached, describe what was observed, and hold the standard regardless of who is in the room. Which norm from today will you use in your next difficult conversation — and when?”

parts.title: 5.3 — Exercise Output
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE
During the presentations, capture the strongest norm from each value set on a shared board. Close by asking the group which patterns appear across the sets.
content: Each participant leaves with three things:
◆ Outputs
Three draft COC norms from their chosen value set — named, acronym-based, and observable
One test commitment — which norm will they reference in their next performance or accountability conversation?
A review date — when will they bring the draft COC to their team for pressure-testing and input?

parts.title: Facilitator · Complete COC for All Three Sets
guidance: ◆ For Facilitator Use Only

These are the complete worked COC entries for all three value sets. Use during and after the debrief to coach, compare, and affirm participant outputs. Do not distribute before teams have completed their own translation work.
content: VALUE SET A — The Governance-Led Organisation
Transparency
OPEN
Own the information flow · Publish decisions with rationale · Enable informed action at every level · Name what you know before being asked

Transparency is the discipline of ensuring that the people who need information to make good decisions have it — before they have to ask for it. A leader operating under OPEN shares context to accelerate the organisation.
360 indicator: Does this leader proactively share information that affects others' ability to act — or do people frequently discover things they needed to know from other sources?
Courage
ACT
Advance the difficult conversation · Challenge the comfortable consensus · Take the harder right over the easier wrong
Courage in leadership is the decision to act despite fear — to name what needs to be named, challenge what needs to be challenged, and hold a position when pressure to abandon it is highest.
360 indicator: Does this leader raise difficult issues in forums where they can be resolved — or after those forums in corridors where they cannot?
Service
FIRST
Find the need before the request · Invest in outcomes · Respond before the follow-up · Stay until the problem is resolved · Treat the person behind the task
Service is the proactive commitment to understanding what the person in front of you actually needs and prioritising that above what is easy to provide.
360 indicator: Does this leader's team feel genuinely served — or do they feel processed?
Resilience
HOLD
Hold the standard under pressure · Observe what is breaking without defensiveness · Learn from every gap · Drive the rebuild without losing the lesson
Resilience is the discipline of maintaining the standard when conditions make it difficult and leading the restoration without losing the lesson embedded in the breakdown.
360 indicator: When things go wrong, does this leader maintain standards and extract learning — or do standards quietly drop until the pressure passes?
Innovation
TEST
Think beyond the obvious solution · Experiment with discipline and a clear hypothesis · Scale what the evidence supports · Terminate what the evidence contradicts
Innovation is the structured discipline of asking whether there is a better way, testing that hypothesis with rigour, and scaling the answer when the evidence supports it.
360 indicator: Does this leader create conditions where ideas are tested and evaluated — or immediately adopted without evidence or dismissed without consideration?
Stewardship
GUARD
Govern resources as if they belong to others · Use with intention and documented rationale · Account for every allocation publicly · Restore what you consume · Decide with the next generation in mind
Stewardship is the recognition that we are custodians — of people, capital, reputation, and the organisation's future. A leader operating under GUARD governs resources as a public trust.
360 indicator: Does this leader make resource decisions they would be comfortable explaining publicly — with full rationale?
VALUE SET B — The Performance-Led Organisation
Trust
EARN
Evidence your commitments with consistent follow-through · Acknowledge gaps before being asked · Return to reliability every time · Name the repair when trust is broken
Trust is built through the accumulation of small, consistent acts of reliability — and rebuilt the same way after it is broken.
360 indicator: When this leader makes a commitment, does the team expect it to be kept — or build informal contingency plans for when it is not?
Agility
MOVE

Monitor signals before they become crises · Override the plan when evidence demands it · Validate the adjustment before treating it as permanent · Execute the pivot with the same discipline as the original plan
Agility is the discipline of reading signals early, making evidence-based course corrections quickly, and confirming the adjustment is working before treating it as permanent.
360 indicator: Does this leader adjust course based on evidence — or maintain original plans in the face of contradicting signals?
Quality
RIGHT

Raise the standard before delivery · Inspect every commitment before it leaves your hands · Give nothing less than your best work · Hold others to the same standard with respect · Treat quality as a habit
Quality is the commitment to setting and holding a standard before delivery.
360 indicator: Does work leaving this leader's function consistently meet the standard the organisation promises — or does quality vary based on workload?
Ownership
MINE

Make the outcome yours regardless of function · Identify the gap and move to close it · Never pass a problem you have the ability to address · Escalate only what genuinely requires authority beyond your own
Ownership is the refusal to let a problem persist because it technically belongs to another function.
360 indicator: Does this leader take action on problems outside their formal remit — or wait for the right person to own them while the problem grows?
Growth
REACH

Recognise the current limit without defensiveness · Engage the discomfort of development deliberately · Assess progress against a measurable standard · Commit to being demonstrably better than last quarter · Hold others' growth as a personal leadership responsibility
Growth is the ongoing commitment to expanding what you and your team can do — holding yourself accountable for measurable progress.
360 indicator: Is this leader's team measurably more capable than six months ago — and can the leader point to specific investments they made to produce that growth?
Inclusion
HEAR
Hold space for every voice in the room · Examine your assumptions before they become decisions · Actively represent perspectives beyond your own · Redesign the process when you discover it excludes
Inclusion is the active discipline of ensuring that different voices are heard and that decisions reflect perspectives of those not always in the room.
360 indicator: Do people different from this leader feel genuinely heard in their forums — or present but not influential?
VALUE SET C — The Purpose-Led Organisation
Purpose
WHY
Work from the mission not the motion · Hold the long view when short-term pressure mounts · Yield personal comfort when purpose requires it
Purpose is the anchor that determines which trade-offs are acceptable and which are not. When purpose and pressure conflict, purpose wins.
360 indicator: When short-term pressures mount, does this leader make decisions that protect the mission — or decisions that protect their position?
Integrity
WHOLE

Walk the same in private as in public · Honour every outcome intended or not · Own consequences without deflection · Leave every situation better than you found it · Expect of yourself what you expect of others
Integrity is the commitment to being the same person in every context — consistent in values when observed and when not.
360 indicator: Does this leader hold the same standard of conduct in a one-to-one conversation as they do in a board presentation?
Ubuntu
WE
Witness the humanity in every person before addressing the task · Extend belonging deliberately to those at the margins of the room

Ubuntu is the recognition that a person is a person through other people. Every action either strengthens or weakens the collective — choose to strengthen it, even when doing so requires personal cost.
360 indicator: Does this leader's team feel seen as people first — or primarily as delivery units?
Excellence
RAISE

Reach beyond the comfortable standard · Assess the evidence of your actual performance honestly · Invest in closing the gap between capability and delivery · Set the bar from what the mission demands · Elevate others as you elevate yourself
Excellence in a purpose-driven organisation is the gap between what we are capable of and what we are currently delivering to those we serve.
360 indicator: Does this leader set standards based on what the mission demands — or on what is comfortable to achieve?
Boldness
DARE

Define the ambitious outcome before negotiating it down · Advance despite uncertainty · Recalibrate with courage when evidence demands a change · Embrace the discomfort of the frontier as a leadership condition
Boldness is the discipline of setting goals that require growth and then doing the work.
360 indicator: Does this leader set goals that stretch the organisation toward its mission — or goals that are safely achievable?
Care
TEND

Take notice of what is wearing people down before they signal it · Engage the human before the task in every significant interaction · Never let urgency override dignity · Deliver results in a way that sustains the people who produce them

Care is the structural commitment to ensuring that the people who carry the mission are themselves sustained. Protect people as fiercely as you protect outcomes — because without the people, there are no outcomes.
360 indicator: Is this leader's team sustainably resourced, psychologically safe, and genuinely developed — or is delivery being achieved through personal sacrifice?

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ Facilitator Closing Note

Close by asking each leader to name one ESRG condition that has been misaligned in their organisation for more than two quarters — visible, discussed, but not yet addressed. Ask them: “What has that misalignment actually cost in strategic momentum? And what is the real reason it has not been restored?” The answers to the second question are almost always the true friction beneath the friction. That conversation is the beginning of genuine Grounding.
content: Unit 10 addresses the question that most strategy execution frameworks never ask directly: Is the organisation itself — its environment, its systems, its resources, its governance — actually built to sustain the performance it is being asked to deliver?
Awareness — What

ESRG Alignment examines the four domains that collectively determine whether performance can be sustained. The Cultural Operating Code is the most important output of the Environment domain: the behavioural architecture of the organisation. Values embedded in 360-degree feedback, enforced through consequences, and modelled by leadership before being expected of teams. The COC turns values into the standard.
Intelligence — Why

ESRG alignment drives sustained execution because each domain removes a specific category of friction. The ignition point of Grounding is reached when all four domains work together as a coherent operating system that reinforces the strategy. At that point, execution no longer depends on heroic individual effort. The organisation's own design carries the work forward.
Extrapolating — Where

Execution friction follows predictable patterns in each domain — values misalignment and psychological safety failures in Environment; workarounds and data fragmentation in Systems; capability gaps and unsustainable workloads in Resources; selective accountability and absent leadership in Governance. Recognising these patterns early is about gaining the organisational intelligence required to strengthen the enterprise.
Integration — Collective

Because ESRG friction rarely stays within a single function, alignment cannot be owned by a single leader. The Execution Muscle Scan — conducted quarterly, immediately after performance results are reviewed — transforms individual functional observations into collective intelligence. The output: the Enterprise ESRG Alignment Agenda. A leadership instrument for proactive execution architecture.

Grounding is where strategy execution is sustained. The environment must enable. The systems must streamline. The resources must sustain. The governance must discipline. When all four are working together — coherently, continuously, and in direct service of the strategic direction — the organisation executes its strategy and becomes capable of executing the next one, and the one after that.
That is an organisational superpower.

top: Grounding asks a harder question: whether the organisation itself is built to sustain this performance over time. ESRG Alignment is the discipline of ensuring that Environment, Systems, Resources, and Governance are fully equipped to support consistent delivery.

parts.title: 1.1 — ESRG Alignment: The Grounding Question
content: Enterprise alignment is one of the most decisive success factors in strategy execution. Performance is sustained by the organisational system: the environment people work in, the systems they rely on, the resources they are given, and the governance structures that guide decisions.
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Most strategies that survive the first quarter fail by the third. What does that tell you about where execution actually breaks down in your organisation?

content: E
Environment
Dim 1

Dim 2
Behavioural
Infrastructure
Reliable connectivity, equipment and working spaces
Business continuity provisions
Workspace Design
Layout reducing delays between dependent roles — proximity is a performance variable
Visual signals reflecting current strategic priorities
Operational Conditions
Remote and hybrid staff participating equally — two-tier participation creates two-tier accountability
Values

Embedded in 360-degree feedback — assessing how as well as what

Cultural Operating Code

Explicit, modelled, reinforced, and reviewed periodically
Psychological Conditions
Psychological safety so people surface problems early
Culture is either taught or it defaults

Core processes documented, current, and easy to find
A trusted single source of truth for key operational data
Teams can see where work sits in the end-to-end process
Systems communicate to eliminate duplicate work
Approvals simple, time-bound, and traceable within the system
R
Resources
Staffing levels supporting normal and peak demand — burnout is a strategic risk
Skills matching current work requirements; talent planning anticipating future needs
Training accompanying every change in process, system, or strategic direction
Budget available for critical strategic initiatives
Teams able to signal unsustainable workloads early
G
Governance
Each area of strategic work has a clearly assigned owner

parts.title: 1.3 — ESRG Synthesis
content: Environment → enables the behavioural and physical conditions for productive, safe, values-aligned work
Systems → enable efficient, visible, and coordinated execution flow
Resources → provide the human, financial, and operational capacity to deliver
Governance → ensures accountability, decision discipline, and execution oversight

The organisation's sustained execution capacity depends on the synchronisation of these four domains. A weakness in any one domain creates friction that the other three cannot fully compensate for. The discipline of ESRG Alignment is the discipline of ensuring all four are working together — coherently, continuously, and in direct service of the strategic direction.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: Why ESRG Alignment Drives Sustained Execution
sections.sub: How each domain removes a specific category of friction — and two worked examples.
slo: Explain how each organisational domain removes a specific source of friction from execution.
Assess where operating conditions support or constrain strategic priorities.

parts.title: 2.1 — The ESRG Ignition Point: How Each Domain Enables Execution
content: E
Enable
S
Streamline
R
Resource
G
Govern
Enable the Work — Physical & Behavioural

Values enable performance when they are demonstrable, measured, and enforced. They create a behavioural environment where conduct is as consequential as results. The Cultural Operating Code translates values into named, actionable norms — moving values from aspiration to operation. Psychological safety completes the enabling condition.
Streamline the Flow

Systems provide pathways through which information, tasks, and decisions move. When clear and reliable, teams can see where work sits, how it progresses, and what action is required. Streamlined systems make execution visible — and visibility is the precondition for accountability.
Resource the Strategy

Teams must possess the skills required, the capacity to sustain effort, and the tools to operate efficiently. Burnout degrades execution quality, accelerates talent exit, and erodes institutional knowledge that is often the organisation's most critical and least recoverable asset.
Govern the Rhythm

Governance provides the structure maintaining the rhythm of decisions, reviews, and accountability. The governance system must apply standards consistently regardless of seniority — leaders exempt from accountability destroy governance credibility faster than any single operational failure.
"When all four conditions operate together, execution no longer depends on leadership attention. The organisation’s operating system reinforces the work itself. That is Grounding."
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Which enabling condition is weakest in your organisation right now — and what is the execution cost?

parts.title: 2.2 — Worked Example 1: The IBSL Cultural Operating Code
content: IBSL’s values: Intentionality · Integrity · Collaboration · Accountability · Excellence · Human-Centricity
Intentionality
Leading with purpose, clarity, and discipline
AIM
Act with purpose · Interrogate assumptions · Maintain the discipline
Intentionality is the discipline of knowing exactly why you are doing what you are doing, and holding that line when conditions make it inconvenient.
Reflect: Before your last three major commitments — could you articulate the strategic purpose, the assumption you were making, and the standard you held yourself to?
Integrity
Consistency between words, behaviour, and outcomes
SAY
Say what you mean · Act on what you say · Yield the truth regardless of consequence
Integrity is about consistency between word, behaviour, and outcome — even when telling the truth is uncomfortable. What we say and what we do are the same thing. Always.
Reflect: In your last performance review — did you name what was promised, what was delivered, and what the gap cost — before being asked?
Collaboration
Leveraging diversity of thought and collective intelligence
ONE
Own a shared outcome · Navigate difference with respect · Execute as a unified force
Collaboration is the decision to produce something together that no single function could produce alone. The result belongs to the team.
Reflect: In your last cross-functional review — did you present the shared outcome, or only your function’s contribution?
Accountability
Owning results and reinforcing transparency
OAR
Own it · Act on it · Report it
Accountability begins the moment a commitment is made. We report the truth and fix the gap.
Reflect: When did you last surface a gap before being asked — with the cause, the impact, and the recovery action already identified?
Excellence
Upholding rigour, learning, and measurable impact
SET
Set the standard · Earn the evidence · Transform through learning
Excellence is a daily discipline. It means being better than last quarter, and proving it with evidence.
Reflect: At your last review — could you answer: What standard did we set? What evidence do we have? What have we changed as a result?
Human-Centricity
Placing people at the core of leadership and execution
SEE
See the person behind the role · Enable growth deliberately · Ensure dignity in every interaction
Leadership serves people. We invest in growth. We protect dignity. We never reduce a person to their output.
Reflect: In your last performance conversation — did you open with the person before moving to the result?

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.h2: Where Are the ESRG Friction Zones?
sections.sub: Recognising the predictable friction patterns in each domain.
slo: Recognise the institutional constraints and dependencies that create friction in each domain.
Determine the type of intervention each constraint requires.

parts.title: 3.1 — E · Environment Friction
content: Physical Friction
Teams asked to work in new ways — cross-functional, faster, hybrid — yet workspaces still reflect older patterns. The execution cost is real and largely invisible in any performance report.
Behavioural Friction

When stated values are not translated into observable behaviours and not embedded in performance measurement, they function as decoration. The absence of a Cultural Operating Code means cultural expectations remain implicit — interpreted differently by different people at different seniority levels. That inconsistency is friction.

When psychological safety fails, execution issues surface too late. The organisation loses its most valuable early warning system: the willingness of people to tell the truth about what is actually happening.
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Which environmental friction pattern — physical or behavioural — is most present in your function right now? What is the execution cost?

parts.title: 3.2 — S · Systems Friction
content: Workarounds invented to keep work moving become, over time, the de facto system. Data integrity is an execution problem. When leaders spend more time debating the accuracy of information than interpreting what it means, systems are failing execution.
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Where in your organisation have workarounds become so normalised that they are now the de facto system?

parts.title: 3.3 — R · Resources Friction
content: The assumption of readiness is itself a source of friction. Burnout is a strategic risk — it degrades execution quality, accelerates talent exit, and erodes institutional knowledge. The absence of a signal that workloads are unsustainable is evidence that psychological safety is insufficient. Strategy follows resources: where the money goes is where the organisation’s real priorities reside.
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Where in your strategy portfolio is there a gap between what you have committed to deliver and what you are actually resourced to achieve?

parts.title: 3.4 — G · Governance Friction
content: Governance structures designed to control risk can begin to slow execution speed as strategy evolves. Selective enforcement — when high performers are exempt from accountability by virtue of results — delegitimises the governance system. A governance system that lacks legitimacy cannot sustain the execution discipline the strategy requires.
✎ Reflection
prompts: ✎ Reflection — Where in your governance system is selective enforcement visible? What signal is that sending to the rest of the organisation?

parts.title: 3.5 — Seeing Friction as Organisational Intelligence
content: Recognising these friction patterns is about gaining operational intelligence.
Values misalignment in the environment signals a gap between cultural aspiration and cultural reality
Systems fragmentation signals an infrastructure built for a different strategic era
Capacity constraints signal a resource allocation that has not yet caught up with strategic ambition
Governance inconsistency signals a leadership system not yet operating at the standard the strategy demands

The role of the executive team is to transform those insights into targeted alignment actions that restore the conditions required for sustained performance — so that execution becomes a function of organisational design.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.sub: The Execution Muscle Scan — transforming individual observations into collective intelligence about execution readiness.
slo: Demonstrate an enterprise view of the operating conditions required for sustainable performance.
Formulate an enterprise agenda for aligning operating conditions with strategic priorities.

parts.title: 4.1 — The Execution Muscle Scan
content: In a mountain expedition, climbers periodically stop to assess whether the conditions around them still support a safe and successful ascent. They check the terrain, the equipment, the team's condition, and the route ahead. The purpose is to ensure the expedition remains properly equipped to continue the climb.

The Execution Muscle Scan is a structured leadership conversation conducted during the quarterly progress review, immediately after performance has been examined. The executive team shifts its attention from outcomes to the conditions that enable those outcomes.
“Are the organisational conditions still supporting our ability to continue the climb?”

Through this process, the executive team transforms operational observations from across the organisation into collective intelligence about execution readiness — and identifies where the enterprise system must be strengthened before the next execution cycle begins.

parts.title: 4.2 — The Four Reflections
content: "Are the organisational conditions still supporting our ability to continue the climb?"
E
Environment
S
Systems
R
Resources
G
Governance

Can teams reach one another quickly? Are hybrid participants fully engaged — or experiencing two-tier participation? Are values being demonstrated? Is the Cultural Operating Code being actively reinforced? Do people feel safe enough to surface execution problems early?
"Do the physical and behavioural conditions make it easy for people to collaborate, speak honestly, and advance the work?"

Are processes remaining clear and accessible — or have workarounds accumulated? Are data sources trusted across functions? Is workflow visibility sufficient — or is execution progress only visible through informal channels?
"Do our systems allow work, data, and decisions to move smoothly and visibly across the organisation?"

Do teams possess the skills required for the current phase? Are staffing levels sufficient? Is financial investment continuing to flow to strategic priorities? Can people signal unsustainable workloads early?
"Do our teams have the capability, capacity, and sustainability required to deliver the strategy over time?"

Are decision rights clear at every level? Are review forums functioning as decision forums — or reverting to status update sessions? Are accountability standards applied consistently regardless of seniority or results?
"Are decisions, accountability, and ethical standards operating at the pace and consistency required to sustain execution?"

parts.title: 4.3 — The COMPASS-ESRG Connection
content: COMPASS Zone | Primary ESRG | Friction Source
Clarity of Direction | Governance | Decision rights unclear; leadership avoiding trade-offs
Organisational Alignment | Environment | Values misalignment; cultural norms fragmented
Management Discipline | Governance | Review forums producing reports not decisions
People & Capability | Resources | Capability gaps; capacity constraints; sustainability failing
Allocation of Resources | Resources | Budget following history
Systems & Execution | Systems | Legacy processes; data fragmentation; shadow systems
Sensing & Adaptation | Environment + Systems | Psychological safety absent; feedback loops broken

parts.title: 4.4 — Collective Signal Intelligence & The Outcome
content: The power of the Execution Muscle Scan lies in how it combines signals from across the executive team into a shared picture of execution readiness. An operational challenge visible to one executive may reflect a systems issue identified by another. A capability concern raised by one function may connect to a governance constraint recognised by another. A values misalignment observed in one team may be a downstream consequence of a leadership behaviour pattern that is visible across multiple functions — but only named when leaders look at the picture collectively.

When those signals are shared in the structured format of the scan, they reveal patterns that individual leaders cannot see alone. Individual observation becomes collective intelligence — a shared understanding of where the organisation's execution conditions must be strengthened before friction compounds into failure.

The output is a Collated Executive View — a shared picture of where the organisation's ESRG conditions are strong, where they are straining, and where targeted intervention is required before the next execution cycle begins.

parts.title: 5.2 — The Exercise (55 minutes)
content: Part 1 · 5 min
Choose
Part 2 · 35 min
Build
Part 3 · 15 min
Challenge
Choose Your Value Set

Select one of the three value sets. Work through three values from your chosen set. Choose the three that feel most relevant or most challenging to translate. Present your strongest single norm to the full group.
Build the COC — Three Steps Per Value
Step 1 — Define the behaviour: What would a leader who genuinely lives this value do differently from one who only states it?
Step 2 — Build the acronym: Take the first letter of three action words. Each must be an observable action — a verb the leader performs.
Step 3 — Write the norm statement: One sentence specific enough that a new employee on Day 1 would know exactly what behaviour will be recognised and what will be corrected.
Capture your three draft norms in the Build Your Cultural Operating Code block below — it stays visible as you work through the steps.
The COC Challenge — Present Your Strongest Norm
Test 1 — The New Employee Test
"If a new employee read this norm on their first day, would they know exactly what behaviour will be recognised and what will be corrected?"
Test 2 — The Pressure Test
"Does this norm hold when a senior leader violates it? Or does it only apply to junior staff?"
Test 3 — The Mirror Test
"Would every person in this room be comfortable being assessed against this norm in their own 360-degree feedback?"
"A Cultural Operating Code only becomes real the moment a leader uses it in a difficult conversation. Which norm from today will you use in your next difficult conversation — and when?"

parts.title: Unit Summary
content: Grounding is where strategy execution is sustained. The environment must enable. The systems must streamline. The resources must sustain. The governance must discipline. When all four are working together — the organisation executes its strategy and becomes capable of executing the next one, and the one after that.
That is an organisational superpower.
